claims.text: Replacing TOR-TILD's empirical EAM reference with an actively trained DNN potential tailored to high-temperature liquid configurations will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The target material is equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi undergoing a near-melting solid-to-liquid transition.
An actively trained DNN potential can be constructed from ab initio molecular-dynamics configurations containing both crystalline and liquid states.
The actively trained DNN potential can serve as a reference potential for thermodynamic integration.
The method is applicable to multicomponent high-entropy alloys over approximately 0.95 to 1.05 times their melting temperature.
Active learning can tailor an interatomic-potential training set to the relevant class of systems, properties, and configurational space.
Training on diverse liquid configurations captures configurational richness that standard EAM models fail to represent.
The DNN will accurately model the many atomic configurations present in the ab initio liquid.
More accurate representation of liquid configurations will improve phase-space overlap between the reference and target ab initio systems.
Improved phase-space overlap will produce a smoother and shorter thermodynamic-integration path.
The DNN reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The DNN-reference calculation will converge free energies to within approximately 5 meV/atom of ab initio values.
Current TOR-TILD calculations using empirical EAM references exhibit significant liquid-state path mismatch because they insufficiently represent the liquid configurational space.
The approach should transfer to other high-entropy alloys with high-temperature liquid disorder similar to CoCrFeMnNi.
Applicability to compositions with markedly different atomic interactions remains unvalidated.
Comparable 30–50% improvements have been observed in elemental and binary systems using machine-learning potentials.
The magnitude of improvement may vary with training-data diversity and alloy-specific characteristics.
A parallel comparison against the standard TOR-TILD EAM reference over 0.95–1.05 times the melting temperature can test the intervention.
Failure to reduce path mismatch by at least 30% or failure to reach approximately 5 meV/atom agreement with ab initio free energies would falsify the hypothesis.
